history.heading: Colony and slavery
paragraphs: Martinique, a volcanic island in the Lesser Antilles, was inhabited by Arawak and then Kalinago peoples. France colonised it in 1635, and sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans made it a valuable colony. Joséphine de Beauharnais, Napoleon's first wife, was born there. Slavery was abolished in 1848 after an uprising on the island.
In 1902 the eruption of Mount Pelée destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre, then the island's largest city, killing about 28,000 people.

history.heading: Overseas department
paragraphs: Martinique became an overseas department of France in 1946, a status championed by the poet Aimé Césaire. Protests over the high cost of living erupted in 2009 and again in 2024. Pollution from the pesticide chlordecone is a major health and political issue.

culture.heading: Négritude and Creole culture
paragraphs: French is official, and Martinican Creole is widely spoken. Martinique gave rise to the Négritude movement, led by Aimé Césaire, and to influential thinkers Frantz Fanon and Édouard Glissant.

Music includes biguine, mazurka and zouk, made famous by the band Kassav'. Carnival is a major celebration. Martinique's agricultural rum (rhum agricole) has a protected designation of origin. Accras and colombo are popular dishes.

politics.heading: Part of France
paragraphs: Martinique is a single territorial collectivity of France and part of the European Union, governed by an elected assembly and executive council. It elects members to the French parliament. Some political movements favour greater autonomy.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: The economy relies on public services, tourism, and agriculture, especially bananas and rum. Most goods are imported, so prices are much higher than in mainland France. Unemployment is high, and many young people emigrate. The currency is the euro.
